entries.name: Common bottlenose dolphin
entries.migrates: seasonal inshore-offshore and latitudinal movements in some populations
behaviour: rides bow waves of boats
cooperative fish-herding hunts
individual signature whistles for identification

voxel_model.pattern: countershaded grey back and pale belly

entries.notes: The benchmark smart sea mammal; superpods of 1,500 have been seen offshore. Not edible by law almost everywhere, so no meat drops in a real-economy build.

entries.name: Killer whale
entries.migrates: follows prey along the coasts and through the open ocean
behaviour: matriarchal pods with dialect-specific call repertoires
pods specialise on different prey and rarely mix
deliberately beaches itself to snatch seals, then slides back

voxel_model.pattern: black and white saddle and eye patches

entries.notes: The ocean's apex social predator; ecotype-specific pods (fish-eaters vs mammal-hunters) behave like different species. Model the dorsal fin: the male's reaches nearly 2 m.

entries.name: Humpback whale
entries.migrates: between polar feeding grounds and tropical calving grounds every year
behaviour: acrobatic breaching and tail-lobbing
bubble-net feeding coordinated by pods
long complex songs from males in breeding grounds

voxel_model.pattern: dark back, white flipper undersides, knobbly head

entries.notes: The most breach-happy big whale; breaching splashes should carry sound and water particles. Its 16 m call to a 1 m player is the single most humbling scale cue in the game.

entries.name: Blue whale
entries.migrates: between polar feeding grounds and tropical breeding grounds every year
behaviour: gulps up to 90 tonnes of water per feeding pass
calls at 188 decibels, among the loudest sounds on Earth
bears 30 cm long ventral groove pleats

voxel_model.pattern: mottled blue-grey, speckled flanks

entries.notes: Largest animal that has ever lived, outmassing any dinosaur. A blue whale's heart and artery are big enough to crawl through; scale everything up to sell it.

entries.name: Sperm whale
entries.migrates: males range poleward; females stay in warm waters year-round
behaviour: dives deeper than any other mammal (2000+ m)
hunts giant squid and octopus in the dark
matriarchal female-and-calf pods, males wander alone

voxel_model.pattern: blocky square head, wrinkled grey skin

entries.notes: The deep-diving leviathan; its 18-m head is nearly a third of body length. Ambergris (a digestive secretion) is the most valuable drop in this file.

entries.name: Beluga whale
entries.migrates: follows the edge of the Arctic sea ice between summering and wintering grounds
behaviour: extremely vocal 'canary of the sea'
turns white as an adult; calves are born grey
can bend its neck, unlike other whales

voxel_model.pattern: pure white adult, melon-shaped forehead

entries.notes: The white Arctic whale; domed melon makes it instantly recognisable. Cold, shallow coastal seas: an Arctic start-game species.

entries.name: Narwhal
entries.migrates: follows the Arctic ice edge between summering and wintering grounds
behaviour: males grow a spiralled left canine up to 3 m long
mottled grey-black and white camouflage from birth
lens-dated, some females may live past 100

voxel_model.pattern: mottled black-on-white, straight spiralled tusk

entries.notes: The unicorn whale; the tusk is a tooth, not a horn, and mostly grows on males. Lens-dating studies suggest some females live past 100, so treat ages above 50 as real possibilities.

entries.name: Harbor seal
behaviour: hauls out on rocks and beaches to rest and pup
spyhops to survey the surface
spotted coat varies hugely between individuals

voxel_model.pattern: spotted, variable blotches on grey or tan

entries.notes: The coast-dwelling seal every harbor knows; haul-outs on rocks are unmissable. Gestation includes delayed implantation, so calendars stretch past 9 months.

entries.name: California sea lion
entries.migrates: seasonal north-south migrations along the Pacific coast
behaviour: barks incessantly at rookeries
stands up on foreflippers like a tripod
curious, intelligent, learns tricks quickly

voxel_model.pattern: uniform dark brown, slightly lighter face

entries.notes: The barking harbor-side performer; bull males stand tall and defend territories on rookeries. Gestation includes a delay of 3-4 months.

entries.name: Walrus
entries.migrates: follows the seasonal Arctic ice edge
behaviour: sucks clams from the seabed with a powerful piston-tongue
uses tusks as anchors, weapons and levers
hauls out in dense noisy herds

voxel_model.pattern: wrinkled rust-brown skin, twin ivory tusks

entries.notes: The Arctic heavyweight; tusks define the silhouette and are a prime ivory drop. Gestation includes delayed implantation, totalling about a year and a half.

entries.name: Sea otter
behaviour: floats on its back cracking shellfish on a stone anvil on its chest
holds hands while resting so they don't drift apart
its dense fur (up to a million hairs per square inch) traps all its insulation

voxel_model.pattern: dark brown body, cream face

entries.notes: The furriest mammal alive and the keystone species that keeps kelp forests free of urchin barrens. Fur drops are historically tempting and notoriously overharvested; delayed implantation means true gestation varies from 4 to 12 months.

entries.name: Leopard seal
entries.migrates: wide-ranging nomadic movements around the Southern Ocean and subantarctic coasts
behaviour: dangerously curious around divers and small boats
pursuit predator of penguins and fur seal pups
reptilian gape; shakes prey side to side to tear it

voxel_model.pattern: reptilian head shape, spotted silver-grey coat

entries.notes: The Antarctic's apex seal and its only true predator of warm-blooded prey; approaching penguins at a beach invites it. Biology poorly studied; breeding data stays null.

entries.name: Great white shark
entries.migrates: huge migrations between coastal hunting grounds and open-ocean 'cafés'
behaviour: breaches completely out of the water striking seals from below
sniffs wounded seals from kilometres away with acute olfaction
patrols seal-colony coasts at dawn and dusk

voxel_model.pattern: grey back sharply countershaded to white belly

entries.notes: The most feared coastal predator on Earth; breach-attacks happen almost exclusively at seal colonies. Recent growth-band research shows they can live 70+ years.

entries.name: Whale shark
entries.migrates: follows plankton blooms between coastal aggregation sites
behaviour: gentle giant that tolerates divers alongside it
gulps 6000 litres of water per hour filtering plankton
spots and stripes form a unique fingerprint per individual

voxel_model.pattern: checkerboard of pale spots and stripes on dark grey

entries.notes: The largest fish alive and entirely harmless to divers; a pregnant female carried ~300 embryos. Longevity unmeasured; live estimates suggest 60-100 years.

entries.name: Tiger shark
entries.migrates: seasonal equatorward-poleward migrations
behaviour: the 'dustbin of the sea' that eats almost anything, including tyres and license plates
nocturnal stalker of shallow seagrass flats
stripes fade with age but remain visible on the flanks

voxel_model.pattern: vertical dark tiger stripes, blunt head

entries.notes: The eating machine; its stomach contents read like a list of everything the sea throws away. Notoriously dangerous to divers in shallow tropical water.

entries.name: Atlantic bluefin tuna
entries.migrates: transatlantic migrations between spawning grounds (Mediterranean, Gulf of Mexico) and feeding grounds
behaviour: cruising schools cross the Atlantic in two weeks
warm-bodied, endothermic: hunts in cold deep water
targeted by industrial fisheries; nearly driven to collapse

voxel_model.pattern: dark blue back, metallic silver belly, yellow finlets

entries.notes: The fastest routine migrant in the Atlantic and the fish the sushi trade almost erased; a 250 kg one is still 'average' for a mature adult. Spawning is external; fertilised eggs drift in the plankton.

entries.name: Swordfish
entries.migrates: seasonal latitudinal migrations between warm seas and cold feeding grounds
behaviour: hunts at night near the surface, rests deep by day
broad flat bill used to slash prey rather than stab
warms its eyes and brain to hunt in icy depths

voxel_model.pattern: dark metallic back, pale belly, no pelvic fins

entries.notes: The billfish of the deep day-night commute; the '60 mph sword' claim is a corruption of an old estimate, so its true top speed stays null. Marvel at bill physics, not speed lore.

entries.name: Atlantic cod
entries.migrates: seasonal migrations to offshore spawning banks
behaviour: demersal: hugs the seabed all its life
broadcasts millions of buoyant eggs that drift to nursery grounds
historically fuelled northern empires; stocks collapsed in 1992

voxel_model.pattern: mottled olive-brown back, white lateral line, one chin barbel

entries.notes: The fish that built the Atlantic; cod liver oil made it a pharmacy staple. The 1992 Canadian collapse is the cautionary tale for any overharvest mechanic.

entries.name: European pilchard (sardine)
entries.migrates: seasonal migrations between inshore feeding and offshore wintering
behaviour: forms spectacular shoals the size of city blocks
filters plankton while swimming with mouth open
the bait-ball that every larger predator in this file eats

voxel_model.pattern: iridescent silver with dark blue-green back, black spot behind gill

entries.notes: The engine of the pelagic food web: every predator in this file runs on pilchards. Shoal rendering is a performance problem worth solving deliberately, not a particle spam.

entries.name: Ocean sunfish
entries.migrates: seasonal migrations following the warm currents carrying its gelatinous prey
behaviour: basks flat on the surface to warm up after deep dives
female may release 300 million eggs in a spawning
flat disk body with no tail to speak of; swims by waving its dorsal and anal fins

voxel_model.pattern: huge grey disk, no true tail

entries.notes: The weirdest large fish alive and the heaviest bony fish on Earth (up to 2.3 tonnes recorded). Basking at the surface is its signature pose; half the world thinks it is dead.

entries.name: Common seahorse
behaviour: male gestates the young in a brood pouch on his abdomen
prehensile tail anchors him to seagrass while he hunts
nimble at colour-matching his surroundings

voxel_model.pattern: yellow-brown, spotted, head coronet

entries.notes: The tail-curled living chess piece; one of the only animal dads with a womb-like pouch. Sold heavily into traditional medicine; each one is a fragile microfauna encounter.

entries.name: Johnson's deep-sea anglerfish
behaviour: female dangles a bioluminescent lure in front of her jaws
male is a tiny parasite that fuses to the female
lives in total darkness at 200-2000 m depth

voxel_model.pattern: black body, glowing lure tip

entries.notes: The deep-sea horror show; only the female is worth modelling big, the parasitic male is a fleck. A bioluminescent lure is a ready-made rare night or deep-cave encounter.

entries.name: Clown anemonefish
behaviour: lives only inside an anemone's stinging tentacles, immune to its venom
the group is a strict size-ordered matriarchy
the largest fish in a group is the female; if she dies, the biggest male becomes female

voxel_model.pattern: bright orange with three white black-edged bands

entries.notes: The aquarium icon; a reef player can keep one in a tiny tank with a host anemone. Sex change on the dominant female's death is a real mechanic worth copying.

entries.name: Leatherback sea turtle
entries.migrates: trans-oceanic migrations between tropical nesting beaches and open-ocean feeding grounds
behaviour: dives deeper than 1000 m; only reptile with its own internal heating
eats jellyfish almost exclusively
nests at night, then returns to the same beach its mother used

voxel_model.pattern: ridged black leathery shell with white spotting

entries.notes: The largest living reptile and the deepest-diving turtle; a living 4 m-leathery missile. Cold-tolerant thanks to gigantothermy; beach nesting is a night-time spectacle.

entries.name: Green sea turtle
entries.migrates: long migrations to natal beaches to nest
behaviour: named for its green cartilage and fat, not its shell
seagrass grazer that keeps seagrass meadows cropped, like a lawnmower
females return to their own birth beach to nest

voxel_model.pattern: smooth olive-brown carapace, often radiating streaks

entries.notes: The gentle vegetarian turtle of seagrass meadows; critical to shallow warm waters. Feminised by warm sand temperatures; many populations sit inside one beach.

entries.name: Wandering albatross
entries.migrates: circumnavigates the Southern Ocean breeding on remote islands, rarely landing otherwise
behaviour: soars for days without flapping on 3.5 m wings
mates for life; pairs perform elaborate courtship dances
incubates 78 days, the longest of any living bird

voxel_model.pattern: white with black wing tips; males whiten with age

entries.notes: The largest wingspan of any bird; 'grandma' specimens reached 60+ years. Dipping within 3 m of the water for days at a time, it is the ship's-shadow icon of southern latitude.

entries.name: Atlantic puffin
entries.migrates: pelagic movements offshore in winter
behaviour: stuffs up to a dozen fish sideways in its beak at once
nests in burrows dug into cliffside turf
stands like a small orange-billed clown on every rock

voxel_model.pattern: black back, white cheeks, rainbow beak

entries.notes: The clown of the cliff, nesting in huge gabbling colonies. Beak-fulls of fish for chicks make excellent inventory-sprite comedy. Harvest bans apply in many regions.

entries.name: Emperor penguin
entries.migrates: walks 50-120 km over sea ice to rookeries each winter
behaviour: males incubate a single egg on their feet under a belly pouch for two months
huddles thousands of males in -40°C gales, rotating outer birds
the deepest-diving bird, reaching 500+ m

voxel_model.pattern: black back, white belly, yellow-orange ear blaze

entries.notes: The only bird that breeds in the dark Antarctic winter; colonies on sea ice are the continent's most moving sight. Huddles rotate so no bird freezes on the outside.

entries.name: Giant Pacific octopus
behaviour: solves puzzles, uses tools and recognizes individual divers
females brood tens of thousands of eggs for six months, then die
can squeeze through any gap wider than its beak

voxel_model.pattern: rust-red with mottled texture, colour-shifts

entries.notes: The most intelligent invertebrate; watches divers, unscrews jars and dies after one brood. Arms stretch to 3 m in old specimens; colour flashes are its language.

entries.name: Mimic octopus
behaviour: impersonates lionfish, sea snakes, flatfish and stingrays
changes body shape, colour and swimming style per threat
the only animal that impersonates multiple species

voxel_model.pattern: banded brown and cream, posture shifts completely

entries.notes: Found in 1998 off Sulawesi and already the most famous octopus alive; ships'-shadow impersonator. Trigger: show it a grouper or a snake model and it should change shape.

entries.name: Giant squid
behaviour: largest invertebrate by length; females may reach 13 m including tentacles
solitary deep hunter; battles with sperm whales leave sucker scars
never reliably filmed alive in the wild until 2006

voxel_model.pattern: reddish-brown; eyes the size of dinner plates

entries.notes: The Kraken's plausible origin; females grow twice the male's size. First live images only in 2006; rare, deep, nocturnal — a legend encounter, not a spawn.

entries.name: Colossal squid
behaviour: heaviest invertebrate: the 495 kg confirmed specimen
ambush predator with swivelling hooks on its tentacles
eyes the size of beach balls, the largest known of any animal

voxel_model.pattern: dark rust mantle, swivelling tentacle hooks

entries.notes: Antarctic, heavier than the giant squid though shorter; only a few have ever been caught intact. Matures in ~2 years from hatchling to half a tonne.

entries.name: Chambered nautilus
entries.migrates: nightly vertical migration between reef slopes (day) and shallower foraging (night)
behaviour: a living fossil: basically unchanged for 500 million years
shell is a buoyancy chamber with ~30 gas-filled compartments
lays only one or two large eggs per year; reproduction glacial

voxel_model.pattern: pinwheel spiral of cream and tiger-stripes

entries.notes: The coiled pinwheel of the deep reef; pop-eyed, ninety-tentacled, utterly ancient. Eggs take up to a year to hatch and adults live 15-20 years; harvests crash fast.

entries.name: American lobster
behaviour: nocturnal bottom-walker with crushing and ripping claws
females carry thousands of eggs under the tail for 9-11 months
molts to grow; old shells are easy to find

voxel_model.pattern: dark olive-brown, mottled

entries.notes: The cold-water delicacy; crusher and ripper claws differ on every individual. Females hang eggs for most of a year, and lobsters live far longer than any tank-label suggests.

entries.name: Blue crab
entries.migrates: seasonal migrations between estuaries and the open shelf
behaviour: swims with paddle-shaped last legs, one of the few swimming crabs
brilliant blue claws on males; red-clawed points on females
females mate only once, carrying sperm the rest of life

voxel_model.pattern: olive-blue shell, electric-blue claws, red fingertips on females

entries.notes: The Chesapeake staple; males are 'jimmies', egg-carriers are 'sooks'. Paddle-swims sideways and upward — a genuinely unusual crab locomotion.

entries.name: Antarctic krill
entries.migrates: daily vertical migrations between depth and surface
behaviour: swarms can exceed two million tonnes — visible from space
can shrink its body during famine to survive shortage
survives without food for up to 200 days

voxel_model.pattern: translucent pink-orange, glowing photophores

entries.notes: The biomass keystone of the Southern Ocean; every blue whale alive is, in a sense, a walking krill cloud. Swarm scale far exceeds anything you can render densely; use imposter rendering.

entries.name: Moon jellyfish
behaviour: four horseshoe-shaped gonads make the 'flower' pattern in the bell
pulses gently upward; blooms in disturbed nutrient-rich water
essentially brainless but steers toward prey by simple sensors

voxel_model.pattern: ghostly transparent with four pink gonads

entries.notes: The safe taste of jellyfish salad and the bell you see in every aquarium; harmless to humans. Blooms signal eutrophication and overfishing — a natural tutorial cue.

entries.name: Portuguese man o' war
entries.migrates: drifts with wind and current; gatherings of thousands pile on windward shores
behaviour: a colony of four specialised polyps, not one animal
floating purple float can exceed 30 cm; tentacles reach 10-50 m
sting causes intense pain; deaths extremely rare but anaphylaxis possible

voxel_model.pattern: translucent purple-blue float, crest on top

entries.notes: The purple sail-of-death; touching one ends a day badly. Windrows of them on a beach are a natural no-entry sign. Tentacle length is the horror stat, not the float.

entries.name: Chironex box jellyfish
behaviour: fastest and most complex jellyfish; swims actively at ~4 m/min
has 24 eyes, including image-forming lenses
its venom stops hearts in minutes; active visual hunter

voxel_model.pattern: almost transparent cube with faint milk-white banding

entries.notes: The most venomous animal on Earth; coastal northern Australia's terror of summer. Seeing its bell means get out of the water; treat any tentacle contact as an emergency.

entries.name: Ochre sea star
behaviour: the textbook keystone predator: pries open mussels with its tube feet
ejects its stomach through the mouth to digest prey outside its body
can regrow entire arms, sometimes whole bodies from a ray

voxel_model.pattern: orange, purple or yellow, heavily textured

entries.notes: Paine's classic keystone species; removing it turns mussel beds into monoculture carpets. The villain of the 2013 sea-star wasting outbreak — a real cautionary mechanic.
